9702-7.2.1.motivate: A rope pulse moves right while the rope moves up and down; sound moves right while air particles move left and right. The direction of particle oscillation distinguishes these waves.
9702-7.2.1.establish: In a transverse wave, particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. In a longitudinal wave, particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer. A wave on a rope is transverse; sound in air is longitudinal. Both kinds transfer energy while particles oscillate about equilibrium, without net movement of the medium. Sound needs a material medium, whereas electromagnetic transverse waves can travel through a vacuum. Transverse waves can be polarised because a transverse vibration direction can be selected; longitudinal waves cannot be polarised in that way. Both types can diffract.
9702-7.2.1.connect: Use the wave terms from 7.1 for either type. Wavelength is still the separation of successive points in phase, even when a longitudinal wave is shown as compressions.
9702-7.2.1.note:
- Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer.
- Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to energy transfer.
- Both transfer energy without net transfer of the medium.
- Sound in air is longitudinal; a rope wave is transverse.
9702-7.2.1.self_explain: A sound wave travels right through air. Describe the motion of one air particle and compare it with a particle on a transverse rope wave travelling right.

9702-7.2.2.motivate: A wavy trace on paper can show sound, even though sound particles do not move up and down. Read what the axes represent before interpreting particle motion.
9702-7.2.2.establish: A displacement–distance graph gives the displacements of many particles at one instant; a displacement–time graph follows one particle. For longitudinal sound travelling right, a vertical graph coordinate can represent horizontal displacement to the right or left. A compression has closer-spaced particles; a rarefaction has wider-spaced particles. Adjacent compression centres or adjacent rarefaction centres are one wavelength apart, and a compression to the nearest rarefaction is half a wavelength. On a right-moving displacement–distance profile, a particle at positive spatial slope initially moves towards negative displacement as the profile shifts right. At a maximum or minimum displacement in sinusoidal motion the particle is momentarily stationary; at zero displacement its speed is greatest. For a longitudinal displacement graph with right positive, a negative spatial slope indicates convergence and compression; positive slope indicates rarefaction.
9702-7.2.2.connect: The wavelength and period from 7.1 link distance snapshots to time traces: one complete spatial cycle is $\lambda$, while one complete temporal cycle is $T$.
9702-7.2.2.note:
- Distance graph: many particles at one time; time graph: one particle over time.
- A longitudinal graph's vertical axis can encode displacement along travel.
- Compression to nearest rarefaction is $\lambda/2$.
- For right-moving waves, particle motion opposes the spatial slope.
9702-7.2.2.self_explain: On a right-moving sound displacement–distance graph, what does a negative spatial slope tell you about particle spacing and the initial motion of a particle there?
